dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Stage one costs almost nothing, and decides almost everything.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: It starts at a desk. Existing geological maps, government survey archives, old company reports, university theses, and the licence register — because ground somebody already holds is not ground you can explore.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: An outcrop is rock in place, and it is the only honest data there is. Everything else is inference. You record what it is, and you record how it is oriented.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Strike is the compass direction of a horizontal line on the surface. Dip is how steeply it leans, and which way.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Three numbers. And they are the most valuable numbers a geologist writes all day, because they tell you where the rock goes when it disappears under the soil.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Then sampling. And the order matters.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Stream sediments first. One sample at the outlet of a catchment represents every rock upstream of it. A handful of silt screens ten square kilometres.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Inside the catchment that came back hot, a soil grid. Lines laid across the strike of the rocks, sampled every twenty-five or fifty metres — because an anomaly running along your grid can hide between two lines.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: And on outcrop, and in trenches, rock chips and channel samples. A continuous cut across the vein, not a hand-picked lump, because picking the best rock is how you lie to yourself.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: A handheld XRF reads some elements on the spot. Excellent for arsenic as a gold pathfinder, and nearly useless for gold itself. Gold goes to a laboratory. Always.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Because arsenopyrite travelled with the gold. You hunt the company it keeps.
